575.title: Jatayu
575.hook: a prince gives a dying bird the rites of a son
575.howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites (antyeshti) are usually performed by a son or close relative; some teachers tell Rama's rites for Jatayu as a sign that loyalty can make someone family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old vulture broke Ravana's bow and chariot, and lost his wings. Wings given for a promise.

Rama comes back from killing the deer, meets Lakshmana on the path, and knows before he gets there. The hut is empty. Valmiki lets Rama come apart. He runs from tree to tree asking where she went. He asks the river. He asks the deer, and the deer turn and look south. His grief turns to rage, and he says he'll tear the worlds apart, until Lakshmana talks him down. Then, on the ground ahead, they see something huge, and bleeding.
screen: `THE EMPTY HUT.` → `THE DEER LOOK SOUTH.` → `SOMETHING ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: At first Rama thinks it's a demon that has eaten Sita, and he draws his bow. Then the bird speaks. It's Jatayu, and he's dying. With what breath he has left, he tells them: Ravana took her. I fought him. He cut me down and flew south. He tries to say more. Valmiki has him begin: Ravana, son of Vishravas, brother of Kubera, the lord of wealth. Then the words stop, and he dies. He spends his last breath the way Sita spent her voice, on the message. Holding the body, Rama tells Lakshmana that this bird lived long in the forest and has died for them, and deserves the same honor as their own father. Remember, Rama wasn't there when Dasharatha's body was burned; he heard the news in the forest, from Bharata. Now Rama builds a pyre himself and performs the last rites for a vulture, as a son would. He offers the water and speaks the verses, and Valmiki says Jatayu goes to the highest worlds. A vulture king's death gets a prince's rites. And the first thing Rama does after learning who took Sita isn't revenge. It's a funeral. Before he hunts the one who took her, he honors the one who tried to save her.

576.title: Kabandha
576.hook: a headless giant with a mouth in its belly and arms that sweep the forest
576.carry: cut the arms, where the strength is
576.howItsDone: Kabandha's encounter is a favorite in storytelling and temple carvings, where he is shown as a headless figure with a face on his belly and long arms.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jatayu's last breath, and a prince who gave a bird a son's funeral. A funeral before revenge.

The brothers head on through deep forest, and the forest gets stranger. Then the path is blocked by something Valmiki describes like a nightmare. It's as big as a hill. It has no head and no neck. Its mouth is in its belly, huge, with teeth. A single eye sits in its chest. And its two arms are so long they sweep the forest around it for anything to eat. Before the brothers can turn, those arms close around them both.
screen: `DEEPER INTO THE FOREST.` → `NO HEAD, A MOUTH IN ITS BELLY.` → `THE ARMS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Its name is Kabandha, and as an ordinary Sanskrit word, kabandha means a headless trunk. The creature squeezes them and says plainly: you'll do for my dinner. Lakshmana is frightened, and Valmiki lets him be. Leave me as its food, he tells Rama. Save yourself, and go find Sita. Rama doesn't take that offer. Instead the brothers look at each other and see the answer at the same moment. The creature's whole strength is in those arms. So Rama cuts off the right arm and Lakshmana the left, with their swords, together, and the giant crashes to the ground. When you're caught, look for where the strength actually is. Then something stranger. Lying there armless, the creature asks who they are. When he hears it's Rama, his tone changes completely. He's glad. He's been waiting for this, he says. He wasn't always like this; there's a story behind the shape, and he'll tell it, but first he'll need one more thing from them. See the pattern of these days. An old bird gives everything. A monster turns out to be waiting for help. Out here, nobody is quite what they look like at first: not the holy man at the door, and not the horror on the path.

577.title: Kabandha
577.hook: the monster's shape was a prank that became a curse
577.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers treat Kabandha's release as a turning point: from here, Rama's search runs through allies in the forest, and the curse ends through Rama's sword and a proper funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha, the headless trunk whose arms swept the forest, brought down by two swords. Cut the arms, where the strength is.
screen: `CUT THE ARMS, WHERE THE STRENGTH IS.`

segments.voice: Lying armless on the forest floor, the creature that tried to eat them sounds almost grateful. Kabandha tells the brothers his story, and it isn't a monster's story at all. Once, he says, he was radiant and beautiful, as bright as the moon. And he had a habit: he liked to put on a terrifying shape and jump out at the sages in the forest, to frighten them. One day he frightened the wrong sage.
screen: `ALMOST GRATEFUL.` → `ONCE, BEAUTIFUL.` → `A PRANK ON THE SAGES.`

segments.voice: The sage was Sthulashira, and he was not amused. Since you love that shape so much, he said, keep it. Kabandha begged, and the sage softened the curse: it would end the day Rama cut off his arms and burned his body in the forest. More trouble followed. Proud of his strength, Kabandha attacked Indra, king of the gods, and Indra's thunderbolt drove his head and thighs down into his body. That's why he has no head. The shape he wore as a joke became the shape he was stuck in. What we pretend to be, the story suggests, can harden into what we are. Then he asks for a funeral. Burn me, he says, and I'll be able to tell you how to find Sita. So once again the brothers build a pyre, this time for a creature who tried to eat them. From the fire, Kabandha rises in a bright form, in shining clothes, in a chariot drawn through the air. And his advice is practical. You need a friend, he tells Rama, someone in trouble like your own. Go to the lake called Pampa and the mountain called Rishyamuka. A monkey named Sugriva lives there, driven out by his brother Vali. Make friends with him; he'll help you search. And on the way, there's an old woman of the forest named Shabari. She's been waiting for you.
screen: `A SAGE'S CURSE: KEEP THAT SHAPE.` · `INDRA'S THUNDERBOLT.` · `BURN ME, AND I'LL TELL YOU.` · `FIND SUGRIVA; VISIT SHABARI.`

578.title: Shabari
578.hook: an old woman of the forest who waited years for one visit
578.howItsDone: Shabari is honored as a model of devotion (bhakti) that needs no rank or learning; the berry story is told in later Ramayanas, songs and sermons, and some temples and festivals honor her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha rose from the fire and pointed the way. Find Sugriva, visit Shabari.

On the western shore of Lake Pampa there's a hermitage that has outlived its teachers. The sages who lived there, disciples of the great rishi Matanga, have all left this world. One person stayed behind: an old woman, an ascetic, living alone among the trees. Before they went, her teachers told her that Rama would come one day, and that she should wait for him. She has been waiting a long time.
screen: `A HERMITAGE BY LAKE PAMPA.` → `THE TEACHERS ARE GONE.` → `ONE WOMAN WAITS.`

segments.voice: Her name is Shabari. Valmiki calls her a shramani, a woman ascetic, and some readers hear in her name the Shabaras, a forest people. When the brothers arrive, she rises, bows at their feet, and welcomes them the way the old texts describe: water for their feet, water to rinse the mouth, a seat. Rama asks what you'd ask any respected elder. Has your practice gone well? Have you mastered anger? Are your vows kept? Is your mind at peace? She answers, in effect: today my practice has borne fruit, because I've seen you. She has gathered forest fruits for him, and she offers them. Look at who is honoring whom. Rama is a prince of Ayodhya. Shabari is an old woman living alone in the forest, with no rank at all. The text makes no speech about it. It just shows a prince sitting in her hermitage, asking about her inner life, and receiving what she gives. Then there's the story told in many homes: Shabari tasted each berry first, so only the sweet ones went to Rama, and he ate them gladly. It isn't in Valmiki. It grew in later tellings, in regional Ramayanas, songs and sermons. In Valmiki she simply offers the fruits she gathered. Both are worth knowing: what the old text says, and what later devotion added.
screen: `SHABARI, A WOMAN ASCETIC.` · `MY PRACTICE HAS BORNE FRUIT.` · `A PRINCE IN A FOREST HERMITAGE.` · `THE TASTED BERRIES: A LATER TELLING.`

579.title: Shabari
579.hook: flowers that never withered, and the forest book closes
579.howItsDone: Shabari's hermitage is remembered at sites near Pampa, by Hampi in Karnataka, and elsewhere; pilgrims visit places linked to her, and the Aranya Kanda is often read or recited as its own unit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari, who waited for years and offered Rama the fruits she'd gathered. My practice has borne fruit, she said.

Shabari's work isn't finished when Rama arrives. She has one more thing to do: show him the place. Here Valmiki's Shabari is less a hostess than a guide, walking the brothers through the forest her teachers left behind. It's the tour an old caretaker gives before handing over a house: this is where the light comes in, this door sticks, this is the room where we used to sing. She isn't showing off. She's making sure the place is remembered properly.
screen: `ONE MORE THING TO DO.` → `A GUIDE, NOT A HOSTESS.`

segments.voice: She shows them Matanga's forest. Here, she says, is the altar where my teachers made their offerings. And look: the flowers they offered haven't withered, after all these years. Here is a place they called the seven seas. When the old sages grew too frail to travel to the sacred waters, they called the seven seas here by the power of their thought. In this telling, a holy place keeps the memory of those who prayed in it. Then Shabari asks Rama's leave. I want to leave this body, she says, and go to the sages I served. Rama gives it. She enters a fire, rises from it radiant, in shining clothes and ornaments, and goes to the world where her teachers are. She had waited for one meeting. When it came, her work was done. And here, beside Lake Pampa, the Aranya Kanda, the forest book, ends. Look at how it ran. Sages in their hermitages. Panchavati. Shurpanakha and the battle with Khara. Maricha's warning and the golden deer. The abduction, Jatayu, Kabandha, and Shabari. It began among sages and ends with a sage's student. In between, nearly everything was lost. Tomorrow a new book opens, the Kishkindha Kanda, by a lake in spring, and someone is about to come down a mountain to talk.
screen: `THE ALTAR, THE UNWITHERED FLOWERS.` · `THE SEVEN SEAS, CALLED BY THOUGHT.` · `SHE RISES FROM THE FIRE.` · `THE FOREST BOOK ENDS.`

580.title: Hanuman's first words
580.hook: a frightened king, two strangers with bows, and a careful messenger
580.howItsDone: Hanuman is worshiped across the Hindu world; in Valmiki he first appears here, as Sugriva's counselor and messenger, and devotees who recite the Kishkindha Kanda meet him in this scene.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari showed Rama her teachers' forest, and the forest book was done. Today the Kishkindha Kanda begins.

Spring at Lake Pampa. Lotuses, bees, birds calling, trees heavy with flowers. And Rama, standing at the shore, finds it unbearable. The Kishkindha Kanda opens on a man surrounded by beauty, and every bit of it reminds him of the person who isn't there. He talks to his brother about it at length, the flowers, the breeze, the birds, and none of it helps. Lakshmana listens for a long time. Then he says, gently, enough. Grief like this will wear you down. Let's go.
screen: `SPRING AT LAKE PAMPA.` → `BEAUTY THAT HURTS.` → `LAKSHMANA: LET'S GO.`

segments.voice: Up on a mountain called Rishyamuka, someone is watching. Sugriva, the exiled monkey prince, sits there with four counselors. He sees two men with bows walking straight toward his hiding place, and he panics: his brother Vali must have sent them to kill him. So the kanda doesn't begin with a hero meeting a hero. It begins with fear. Sugriva is a hunted man, and two strangers with bows look like the end. He turns to his wisest counselor, Hanuman, who calms him first. You're jumping at shadows, he tells him, more or less, and a king who acts on fear before he knows is a weak king. Then Sugriva gives him the job. Go down and find out who they are. Watch their faces, their speech, their manner. Tell me if they mean harm. And Hanuman doesn't go as a monkey. He takes the form of a wandering mendicant, a bhikshu. Sound familiar? Only days ago in the story, Ravana came to Sita disguised as a holy man, to deceive and to steal. Now Hanuman takes nearly the same disguise, to find out the truth and to protect. The same costume, opposite hearts. And look at who Hanuman is in this first scene. Not the giant who leaps the sea, not yet. A careful messenger walking down a mountain, deciding what to say.
screen: `SUGRIVA SEES TWO ARMED MEN.` · `HANUMAN CALMS THE PANIC.` · `A MENDICANT'S DISGUISE.` · `SAME COSTUME, OPPOSITE HEARTS.`

581.title: Hanuman's first words
581.hook: a stranger's sentence so well made that Rama names every virtue in it
581.howItsDone: Devotees honor Hanuman for learning and eloquence as well as strength, and this passage, where Rama praises his grammar and delivery, is one source of that picture.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman walked down the mountain disguised as a bhikshu, a wandering mendicant. Same costume, opposite hearts. Today the week closes.

Have you ever met someone and known within a minute, from how they spoke, that you could trust them? Not from what they said, exactly. From how. Hanuman reaches the brothers and speaks, and when he's finished, Rama turns to Lakshmana and says something remarkable about a stranger's sentence. Remember where Rama is. He has lost his kingdom, his father and now his wife. He has no reason to trust anyone on this mountain. And a few sentences from a stranger change that.
screen: `NOT WHAT, BUT HOW.` → `RAMA TURNS TO LAKSHMANA.`

segments.voice: Hanuman greets them with respect. You look like sages, he says, or like kings: why are you in this forest? Then he tells them who he is: a minister of Sugriva, a monkey king driven out by his brother, who wants their friendship. He's careful and warm, and honest about who sent him. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana, and his praise is precise. Nobody could speak like this, he says, who hadn't learned the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Sama Veda. He has clearly studied grammar well; in all he said, not one word was wrong. Nothing in his face, his eyes or his brow was out of place. He didn't drag it out or rush it. His voice came from the chest and throat, in a middle pitch, clear and pleasing. A king with a messenger like this, Rama says, can get anything done. Notice what Rama praises: not strength, but speech. Good speech here is a kind of goodness, right in length, right in tone, honest about who sent him. And Rama, grieving and exhausted, still notices a stranger's care with words, and says so. Now the week, from the top. Jatayu's last breath and his funeral. Kabandha, and the curse that came from a prank. Shabari, waiting, and the flowers that never withered. Lake Pampa in spring. And today, a sentence that starts a friendship.
screen: `A MINISTER OF SUGRIVA.` · `NOT ONE WORD WRONG.` · `NOT TOO LONG, NOT RUSHED.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `A SENTENCE THAT STARTS A FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Choose one true, kind sentence you might say to someone soon, and say it silently once. Then shape it, a word too many, a tone not quite right, and say it again in your head a little cleaner, until it rests easy.
Vakya, a sentence: what Rama praises when Hanuman speaks, saying no word was wrong, not too long, not rushed.
Your line: not one word wrong. Rama heard a friend in the way a stranger spoke. That's day five hundred eighty-one.
